newsitem.title: USA: Morris says Clinton thought Powell could beat him.
newsitem.headline: Morris says Clinton thought Powell could beat him.

text.p: President Bill Clinton was terrified at the thought of retired Gen. Colin Powell running for president, telling confidants "he'll run a great campaign and he'll beat me bad," Clinton's former top political adviser Dick Morris says in a new book.

Morris, who quit the 1996 campaign in August after being involved in a sex scandal, also says in the book that Clinton thought his Republican opponent Bob Dole was "an evil, evil man." Morris added that Clinton was completely committed to doing all he could to make Vice President Al Gore the Democratic party's presidential nominee in the year 2000.

The book, "Behind the Oval office: Winning the Presidency in the Nineties," will not be published by Random House until next week, but it is already causing a stir in Washington with the White House denying Morris's quotes about Clinton's feelings towards Dole. An advance copy of the book was obtained by Reuters.
In the book, Morris said Clinton phoned him after Elizabeth Dole made a stirring speech supporting her husband at the Republican convention in July.

He quoted Clinton as saying Dole was "an evil, evil man. He likes cutting food stamps ... He enjoys cutting Medicare. He relishes slashing education. He loves cutting immigrants. It's how he gets his kicks."

Asked about the comments published in a late edition Friday of the Washington Post, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton did not feel that way and said he never heard him express such thoughts.
While McCurry could not say definitively that Clinton did not make the remarks, he stressed that the president had often expressed his respect and admiration for Dole.
The press secretary said Clinton had read Morris's book "and thinks parts of it are interesting, parts of it are wrong, parts are factually off the mark, some of it provides insight."
Morris said that the thought of Powell, the first black to be named chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, running for president terrified Clinton.

"The president did not believe he could beat Powell," Morris said, adding that Clinton told him: "He'll take away blacks; he'll separate himself from the Congressional Republicans; he'll run a great campaign and he'll beat me bad."
After Powell bowed out of seeking the Republican nomination, Clinton feared that he might accept the vice presidential nomination from Dole.

"Before the San Diego convention, we had a second Colin Powell scare, this time with speculation that Dole would choose the hero general as his running mate ... the president reacted to Powell as usual: with terror."
Morris also said that Clinton was in chronic conflict with his staff in 1995, writing, "Time and again he would derisively refer to his staff as 'the children who got me elected.'"
